column2: What does an Azure DevOps organisation group administratively?
column3: Projects and shared organisation-level settings, identities, billing and policies.

column2: How do Azure DevOps projects differ from teams?
column3: Projects organise resources and permissions; teams organise work and team settings within a project.

column2: What delivery responsibility belongs to Azure Repos?
column3: Source control, including Git or TFVC, with collaboration and review controls.

column2: What delivery responsibility belongs to Azure Pipelines?
column3: Executing automated build, test and deployment workflows.

column2: What delivery responsibility belongs to Azure Artifacts?
column3: Hosting and sharing packages through feeds with access and lifecycle controls.

column2: What delivery responsibility belongs to Azure Boards?
column3: Planning and tracking work through work items, backlogs and boards.

column2: What delivery responsibility belongs to Azure Test Plans?
column3: Managing manual and exploratory testing, test cases, suites and related results.

column2: How do Azure DevOps Services and Server differ operationally?
column3: Services is Microsoft-hosted and continuously updated; Server is customer-operated, with features tied to the installed release.

column2: Why is a YAML pipeline easier to review alongside code than a classic pipeline definition?
column3: Its definition is a version-controlled file; classic definitions are primarily managed in the service UI.

column2: For Azure Repos Git, does a YAML pr: trigger implement pull-request validation?
column3: No. Configure a build-validation branch policy; YAML PR triggers apply to other supported repository providers.

column2: In Azure Pipelines, how is a task related to a step?
column3: A task is a packaged operation used as a step; steps can also run scripts.

column2: What distinguishes an Azure Pipelines agentless job from an agent job?
column3: An agentless job uses pool: server and only supported server tasks; arbitrary build scripts require an agent.

column2: How should a multi-stage Azure delivery pipeline separate validation from production?
column3: Use explicit build/test/deploy stages, dependencies and protected production resources.

column2: What does an Azure YAML pipeline resource declaration represent?
column3: An external input or dependency, such as another pipeline, repository, container or package.

column2: What configures a downstream Azure YAML pipeline to run when an upstream pipeline succeeds?
column3: A pipeline resource with completion triggering and any required branch, stage or tag filters.

column2: Why include succeeded() in a custom Azure job condition when prerequisite success is required?
column3: A custom condition replaces the default success condition; omitting it can allow execution after failure.

column2: What does including an Azure YAML template do?
column3: Expands reusable steps, jobs, variables or stages into the consuming pipeline at template processing time.

column2: How does Azure YAML extends differ from inserting a steps template?
column3: extends establishes the pipeline's outer structure and permitted parameters; an included template fills a location chosen by the caller.

column2: When should Azure template parameters be used instead of runtime variables?
column3: For typed choices that determine pipeline structure before execution; variables carry string values used during execution.

column2: Are Azure runtime parameters suitable for secrets?
column3: No. Parameters are not secret storage; use secret variables or a supported secret store.

column2: Can an Azure compile-time template expression read a value created by a later task?
column3: No. Template expansion occurs before that task runs.

column2: When do Azure macro variables such as $(name) expand?
column3: Before the consuming task executes; runtime expressions such as $[variables.name] have different evaluation rules.

column2: How should values pass through nested Azure templates?
column3: Each template declares and explicitly forwards the required parameters to the next template.

column2: What should a centrally governed Azure pipeline template control?
column3: Mandatory validation and allowed extension points, with protected-resource checks enforcing its use where required.

column2: Does banning one Azure script task guarantee consumers cannot execute arbitrary code?
column3: No. Other tasks or repository scripts can execute code; restrict extension points and enforce trust and resource controls.

column2: What happens to a Microsoft-hosted Azure agent VM after a job?
column3: It is discarded; each job receives a fresh VM and cannot rely on the previous job's filesystem.

column2: What should determine Windows versus Linux for an Azure self-hosted agent?
column3: Required tools, operating-system APIs and script compatibility, plus the operator's ability to maintain the host.

column2: How do Azure agent pools and project queues relate?
column3: A pool groups agents; a project-level queue references a pool for that project's jobs.

column2: What happens if no Azure self-hosted agent satisfies a job's demands?
column3: The job cannot be assigned to an unsuitable agent; install the capability, correct the demand or select an appropriate pool.

column2: Are an Azure agent's registration identity and job access token the same credential?
column3: No. Registration establishes the agent; job-specific access tokens authorise pipeline resource operations during execution.
